overview: This map uses “Curonians” for 500 BCE to 200 CE, centuries before the fifth- to early sixth-century formation described by Lithuania’s National Museum. The label is therefore retrospective and its outline is not a secure ethnic border. This card explores earlier coastal communities in western Lithuania and southwestern Latvia, using archaeology rather than projecting medieval Curonian sailors into the distant past.

periods.title: Earlier coastal communities
periods.summary: Early Iron Age settlements and burial grounds reveal local ways of building, making objects and remembering the dead.

periods.title: The first two centuries CE
periods.summary: Flat cemeteries and imported Roman objects form part of a changing regional archaeological record.

items.text: At Paplaka in southwestern Latvia, excavators found a building partly sunk into the ground. Its oval hollow measured about 2 by 3 metres, with clay-lined sides and a lower approach to the entrance. Radiocarbon analysis places the building and its finds between 361 and 204 BCE.

About 600 pieces of clay daub came from the Paplaka building. Impressions preserved the shapes of wooden elements, and the excavator suggests clay protected wood near the hearth from fire. A building that disappeared can still leave the imprint of its timbers in a handful of baked clay.

Paplaka also yielded fragments of at least 32 pots, mostly with scratched surfaces. The same building contained pieces of bronze ornaments, an iron hook, a fire-lighting stone and a grooved sandstone whetstone. These small finds place pottery, metal objects and sharpening equipment together in an ordinary working space.

Researchers studying the Akmena River near Kurmaičiai propose that three neighbouring communities used this landscape during the later first millennium BCE and early first millennium CE. They suggest a division between living and farming areas on one bank and burial places on the other. This is a model built from scattered archaeological sites.

Finding a cemetery does not automatically reveal the village beside it. Five test pits on the Akmena’s left bank failed to locate the proposed prehistoric settlement. Ancient field remains nevertheless suggest activity there. Archaeology sometimes produces a useful unanswered question: where exactly did the people who used these graves live?

Regional plant research offers a glimpse of changing farming. Evidence from Lithuania places the arrival of rye and oats around 100 to 200 CE. The study draws largely on inland sites, so these are regional comparisons rather than a shopping list for every coastal household. Charred grains can preserve information that a vanished meal cannot.

Horse remains from Kurmaičiai, Kveciai and Ėgliškės show that animals also had a place in burial ceremonies. A study of Late Bronze and Early Iron Age graves found unburnt parts of horses alongside cremated people. The researchers interpret this as evidence of horses’ special importance, though the bones cannot tell the complete story of each ceremony.

A young person buried at Šlikiai was remembered with an urn and a circle of stones. Radiocarbon testing placed this grave between 396 and 206 BCE. The report identifies a non-adult, rather than claiming an exact age. Even without a surviving name, this carefully recorded grave gives a child or adolescent a place in the story.

At Dauglaukis, a child’s grave contained an iron pin and an amber bead near surviving teeth and skull fragments. Its published date, 70 to 260 CE, extends beyond this map’s endpoint. The excavator also noted possible disturbance. Small ornaments survive here as fragile traces of a particular child, whose name and sex remain unknown.

By the late first and second centuries CE, some western Lithuanian cemeteries used flat graves surrounded by connected stone circles. Earlier burial mounds and cremation traditions had different arrangements. Changes in burial practice help archaeologists distinguish phases, although a new grave style alone cannot prove that an entirely new people arrived.

The long-used Ėgliškiai-Anduliai cemetery yielded Roman coins, including issues of Emperor Hadrian, who ruled from 117 to 138 CE. Such objects connect this Baltic region with wider exchange networks. The date stamped into a ruler’s coin history is not necessarily the date when that coin reached the coast or entered a grave.

Modern laboratory work has tested old assumptions about the burial mounds. A 2022 study dated twelve bone samples from six cemeteries. One supposed prehistoric grave at Kveciai actually dated to 1047 to 1260 CE. People had reused an ancient place much later, a reminder to check the age of each burial separately.

There is no securely identified local written sentence to quote from these early communities. Even the much later Curonian language left no surviving written monuments, according to Lithuania’s language encyclopedia. Archaeological objects help reconstruct daily activities, but cannot supply an ancient child’s exact words. Modern Lithuanian or Latvian would not be a substitute.

ending.text: The year 200 is the end of this imported map record, not a documented destruction. Coastal communities continued changing, and the recognisable medieval Curonian cultural formation emerged centuries later. The early record and medieval Kurs therefore need separate histories.
